Below is a reply from a philosophical exchange, followed by four passages from the same exchange. Which passage is the objection this reply answers? Reply with the letter of one option.

Reply: When I say that an idea is innate in us, or imprinted in our souls by nature, I do not mean that it is always present to us. This would make no idea innate. I mean merely that we possess the faculty of summoning up this idea.

A. It is true that ignorance is merely a defect, and that we stand in need of no special positive faculty in order to be ignorant; but about error the case is not so clear. For it appears that stones and inanimate things are unable to err solely because they have no faculty of reasoning or imagining. Hence it is a very direct inference that, in order to err, a faculty of reasoning, or at least of imagination, is required; and both of these are positive faculties.
B. It is the common belief that no fault is committed by medical men who deceive sick people for their health's sake, nor by parents who mislead their children for their good. The evil in deception lies not in the falsity of what is said, but in the bad intent of those who practise it. One must therefore examine whether the proposition 'God can in no case deceive us', taken universally, is true; for if it is not, the conclusion that corporeal things exist does not follow.
C. I ask whether it is really the case that one who dreams he doubts whether he dreams or no is unable to dream that his dream is connected with the idea of a long series of past events. If he can, those things which to the dreamer appear to be the actions of his past life may be regarded as true just as though he had been awake. Besides, if all certitude depends on knowing the true God, either an Atheist cannot infer from the memory of his previous life that he wakes, or a man can know that he is awake apart from knowledge of the true God.
D. When M. Descartes says that the idea of God and that of the soul are innate in us, I should like to know whether the minds of those who are in a profound and dreamless sleep yet think. If not, they have at that time no ideas. Whence no idea is innate, for what is innate is always present.

Below is a reply from a philosophical exchange, followed by four passages from the same exchange. Which passage is the objection this reply answers? Reply with the letter of one option.

Reply: Here the meaning assigned to the term idea is merely that of images depicted in the corporeal imagination; and, that being agreed on, it is easy to prove that there is no proper idea of Angel or of God. But I have everywhere shown that I take the term idea to stand for whatever the mind directly perceives. So when I will or when I fear, since at the same time I perceive that I will and fear, that very volition and apprehension are ranked among my ideas. I employed this term because it was the term currently used by philosophers for the forms of perception of the Divine mind, though we can discover no imagery in God.

A. When M. Descartes says that the idea of God and that of the soul are innate in us, I should like to know whether the minds of those who are in a profound and dreamless sleep yet think. If not, they have at that time no ideas. Whence no idea is innate, for what is innate is always present.
B. It is true that ignorance is merely a defect, and that we stand in need of no special positive faculty in order to be ignorant; but about error the case is not so clear. For it appears that stones and inanimate things are unable to err solely because they have no faculty of reasoning or imagining. Hence it is a very direct inference that, in order to err, a faculty of reasoning, or at least of imagination, is required; and both of these are positive faculties.
C. When I think of a man, I recognize an idea or image with figure and colour as its constituents. But when one thinks of an Angel, what is noticed in the mind is now the image of a flame, now that of a fair winged child, and this has no likeness to an Angel. It is the same way with the most holy name of God; we have no image, no idea corresponding to it. Hence it appears that we have no idea of God, and a man who reasons back to an eternal cause merely gives a name to the object of his faith or reasoning and calls it God.
D. It is the common belief that no fault is committed by medical men who deceive sick people for their health's sake, nor by parents who mislead their children for their good. The evil in deception lies not in the falsity of what is said, but in the bad intent of those who practise it. One must therefore examine whether the proposition 'God can in no case deceive us', taken universally, is true; for if it is not, the conclusion that corporeal things exist does not follow.

Here are two short passages of philosophical argument. In which passage does the conclusion follow from what comes before? Reply with A or B only.

A. When I consider the mind, that is to say, myself inasmuch as I am only a thinking thing, I cannot distinguish in myself any parts, but apprehend myself to be clearly one and entire. Although the whole mind seems to be united to the whole body, yet if a foot, or an arm, or some other part, is separated from my body, I am aware that nothing has been taken away from my mind. And it is in part so with corporeal or extended objects, for there are some of these imaginable by me which my mind can easily divide into parts. This would be sufficient to teach me that the mind or soul of man is entirely different from the body.

B. When I consider my mind, that is, myself only insofar as I am a thinking thing, I can find no parts in myself, but grasp myself as plainly one and whole. Though the whole mind seems joined to the whole body, if a foot, an arm or some other part is cut off from my body, I know that nothing has been removed from my mind. Bodies, or extended things, are entirely different: I cannot imagine a single one that my mind could not readily divide into parts. That alone would show me that the human mind or soul is wholly distinct from the body.

Below is an objection from a philosophical exchange, followed by four passages from the same exchange. Which passage is the reply to this objection? Reply with the letter of one option.

Objection: It is said that the non-existence of this being is inconceivable. It might better be said, perhaps, that its non-existence, or the possibility of its non-existence, is unintelligible, for according to the true meaning of the word, unreal objects are unintelligible. I am most certainly aware of my own existence; but I know, nevertheless, that my non-existence is possible. Whether, so long as I am most positively aware of my existence, I can conceive of my non-existence, I am not sure; but if I cannot, God will not be the only being of which it can be said that it is impossible to conceive of his non-existence.

A. I was attempting to prove what was still uncertain, and contented myself at first with showing that this being is understood in any way, and is in the understanding. It was my intention to consider, on these grounds, whether this being is in the understanding alone, like an unreal object, or whether it also exists in fact, as a real being. For if unreal objects, or objects whose existence is uncertain, are in this way understood and in the understanding, there is no reason why that being of which I spoke should not be understood and be in the understanding.
B. Your so careful demonstration that the being than which a greater cannot be conceived is not analogous to the not yet executed picture in the understanding of the painter is quite unnecessary. It was not for this purpose that I suggested the preconceived picture. I had no thought of asserting that the being which I was discussing is of such a nature; but I wished to show that what is not understood to exist can be in the understanding.
C. Obviously this is not true. For everything that is less good, in so far as it is good, is like the greater good. It is therefore evident to any rational mind that by ascending from the lesser good to the greater, we can form a considerable notion of a being than which a greater is inconceivable. There is, then, a means of forming a notion of a being than which a greater is inconceivable.
D. It was more proper to say it cannot be conceived. For although no objects which exist can be understood not to exist, yet all objects, except that which exists in the highest degree, can be conceived not to exist. For all those objects, and those alone, can be conceived not to exist, which have a beginning or end or composition of parts. Be assured, then, that you can conceive of your own non-existence, although you are most certain that you exist.

Here are two short passages of philosophical argument. In which passage does the conclusion follow from what comes before? Reply with A or B only.

A. Spiritual power is not lost by mortal sin, for a bad priest consecrates the Eucharist and a bad bishop consecrates a priest. Civil power and spiritual power are exercised over quite different matters. Therefore civil power is not lost by mortal sin either.

B. Mortal sin does not take away spiritual power, since a wicked priest still consecrates the Eucharist and a wicked bishop still ordains a priest. Civil power appears to rest on grace far less than spiritual power does. So mortal sin does not take away civil power either.

Below is a reply from a philosophical exchange, followed by four passages from the same exchange. Which passage is the objection this reply answers? Reply with the letter of one option.

Reply: One who dreams cannot effect a real connection between what he dreams and the ideas of past events, though he can dream that he does connect them; and when he has awakened he will easily detect his error. An Atheist is able to infer from the memory of his past life that he is awake. Still he cannot know that this sign is sufficient to give him the certainty that he is not in error, unless he knows that it has been created by a God who does not deceive.

A. There is a great difference between imagining, that is, having some idea, and conceiving with the mind, that is, inferring as the result of a train of reasoning that something is or exists. But what shall we now say, if reasoning chance to be nothing more than the uniting and stringing together of names or designations by the word 'is'? It will follow that reason gives us no conclusion about the nature of things, but only about the terms that designate them. Thus reasoning will depend on names, names on the imagination, and imagination, perchance, on the motion of the corporeal organs; and so mind will be nothing but the motions in certain parts of an organic body.
B. When I think of a man, I recognize an idea or image with figure and colour as its constituents. But when one thinks of an Angel, what is noticed in the mind is now the image of a flame, now that of a fair winged child, and this has no likeness to an Angel. It is the same way with the most holy name of God; we have no image, no idea corresponding to it. Hence it appears that we have no idea of God, and a man who reasons back to an eternal cause merely gives a name to the object of his faith or reasoning and calls it God.
C. I ask whether it is really the case that one who dreams he doubts whether he dreams or no is unable to dream that his dream is connected with the idea of a long series of past events. If he can, those things which to the dreamer appear to be the actions of his past life may be regarded as true just as though he had been awake. Here are two short passages of philosophical argument. In which passage does the conclusion follow from what comes before? Reply with A or B only.

A. No doctrine can be true that necessarily leads a man into an absurdity. It is an absurdity to think that the same thing should be at the same time both cold and warm. If one hand is hot and the other cold, and both are put at once into the same vessel of water, the water will seem cold to one hand and warm to the other. By the principle that things have in them whatever degree of heat or cold we feel on applying them, we must then conclude that the water is really both cold and warm at the same time. Consequently every principle about heat and cold in bodies is false.

B. A doctrine that unavoidably leads to an absurdity cannot be true. It is absurd to suppose that one and the same thing is cold and warm at once. Suppose one hand is hot and the other cold, and both are dipped together into the same bowl of lukewarm water: the water will feel cold to one hand and warm to the other. By the principle that things contain whatever degree of heat or cold we feel when we touch them, we would have to say the water really is cold and warm at once. So that principle is false.

Below is a reply from a philosophical exchange, followed by four passages from the same exchange. Which passage is the objection this reply answers? Reply with the letter of one option.

Reply: Nor is there any difficulty in what is here alleged about space having parts. For infinite space is one, absolutely and essentially indivisible; and to suppose it parted is a contradiction in terms, because there must be space in the partition itself, which is to suppose it parted and yet not parted at the same time. The immensity or omnipresence of God is no more a dividing of his substance into parts than his duration, or continuance of existing, is a dividing of his existence into parts. There is no difficulty here but what arises from the figurative abuse of the word parts.

A. These gentlemen maintain that space is a real absolute being. But this involves them in great difficulties, for such a being must needs be eternal and infinite. Hence some have believed it to be God himself, or one of his attributes, his immensity. But since space consists of parts, it is not a thing which can belong to God.
B. As for my own opinion, I have said more than once that I hold space to be something merely relative, as time is; that I hold it to be an order of coexistences, as time is an order of successions. For space denotes, in terms of possibility, an order of things which exist at the same time, considered as existing together, without enquiring into their manner of existing. And when many things are seen together, one perceives that order of things among themselves.
C. Space is something absolutely uniform; and, without the things placed in it, one point of space does not absolutely differ in any respect whatsoever from another point of space. Now from hence it follows, supposing space to be something in itself besides the order of bodies among themselves, that it is impossible there should be a reason why God, preserving the same situations of bodies among themselves, should have placed them in space after one certain particular manner and not otherwise; why everything was not placed the quite contrary way, for instance, by changing east into west. But if space is nothing else but that order or relation, then those two states would not at all differ from one another, and there is no room to enquire after a reason of the preference of the one to the other.
D. There is no such thing as two individuals indiscernible from each other. An ingenious gentleman of my acquaintance, discoursing with me in the presence of the Princess Sophia in the garden of Herrenhausen, thought he could find two leaves perfectly alike. The princess defied him to do it, and he ran all over the garden a long time to look for some, but it was to no purpose. Two drops of water, or milk, viewed with a microscope, will appear distinguishable from each other; and this is an argument against atoms.

Here are two short passages of philosophical argument. In which passage does the conclusion follow from what comes before? Reply with A or B only.

A. Whatever things are said to possess an attribute in such a way that in mutual comparison they may be said to possess it in greater, or less, or equal degree, possess it by virtue of something which is the same in the different cases. It is certain that some goods, if mutually compared, would prove either equally or unequally good. Necessarily, then, they are all good by virtue of something which is conceived of as the same in different goods.

B. Whatever things are said to possess an attribute in such a way that in mutual comparison they may be said to possess it in greater, or less, or equal degree, possess it by virtue of something which is the same in the different cases. It is certain that all goods, if mutually compared, would prove either equally or unequally good. Necessarily, then, they are all good by virtue of something which is conceived of as the same in different goods.

Here are two short passages of philosophical argument. In which passage does the conclusion follow from what comes before? Reply with A or B only.

A. Throughout nature, the intricate fitting of means to ends closely resembles, while far surpassing, what human ingenuity produces: the work of human planning, thought, wisdom and intelligence. Because the effects are alike, every rule of analogy leads us to conclude that their causes are alike as well. So the maker of nature is somewhat like a human mind, though with far greater powers.

B. The curious adapting of means to ends, throughout all nature, resembles exactly, though it much exceeds, the productions of human contrivance; of human design, thought, wisdom, and intelligence. Since therefore the effects resemble each other, we are led to infer, by all the rules of analogy, that the causes may be wholly unlike. And so the Author of Nature is somewhat similar to the mind of man, though possessed of much larger faculties.

Here are two short passages of philosophical argument. In which passage does the conclusion follow from what comes before? Reply with A or B only.

A. On putting your hand near the fire, you perceive a sensation that grows stronger as the hand comes closer to it. The heat is immediately perceived. The pain also is immediately perceived, and at the same time as the heat. It follows that the intense heat immediately perceived and the pain are one and the same simple idea.

B. On putting your hand near the fire, you perceive one simple, uniform sensation, and not two distinct sensations. The heat is immediately perceived. The pain also is immediately perceived, and at the same time as the heat. It follows that the intense heat immediately perceived and the pain are one and the same simple idea.

Below is a reply from a philosophical exchange, followed by four passages from the same exchange. Which passage is the objection this reply answers? Reply with the letter of one option.

Reply: I promise confidently that if any man shall devise anything existing either in reality or in concept alone, except that than which a greater cannot be conceived, to which he can adapt the sequence of my reasoning, I will discover that thing, and will give him his lost island, not to be lost again. But it now appears that this being than which a greater is inconceivable cannot be conceived not to be, because it exists on so assured a ground of truth. For if it could be conceived not to exist, it could be conceived to have a beginning and an end; but this is impossible.

A. It is said that the non-existence of this being is inconceivable. It might better be said, perhaps, that its non-existence, or the possibility of its non-existence, is unintelligible, for according to the true meaning of the word, unreal objects are unintelligible. I am most certainly aware of my own existence; but I know, nevertheless, that my non-existence is possible. Whether, so long as I am most positively aware of my existence, I can conceive of my non-existence, I am not sure; but if I cannot, God will not be the only being of which it can be said that it is impossible to conceive of his non-existence.
B. This being is said to be in my understanding already, only because I understand what is said. Could it not with equal justice be said that I have in my understanding all manner of unreal objects, having absolutely no existence in themselves, because I understand these things if one speaks of them, whatever they may be? Unless indeed it is shown that this being is of such a character that it cannot be held in concept like all unreal objects, or objects whose existence is uncertain.
C. Your example of the painter who already has in his understanding what he is to paint cannot agree with this argument. For the picture, before it is made, is contained in the artificer's art itself; and any such thing, existing in the art of an artificer, is nothing but a part of his understanding itself. Hence, even if it were true that there is a being than which a greater is inconceivable, yet to this being, when heard of and understood, the not yet created picture in the mind of the painter is not analogous.
D. It is said that somewhere in the ocean is an island which, because of the impossibility of discovering what does not exist, is called the lost island, and that it is more excellent than all other countries in the abundance of its riches. Now suppose someone went on to say, as if by a logical inference: you can no longer doubt that this island exists somewhere, since you have no doubt that it is in your understanding; and since it is more excellent to exist both in the understanding and in reality, for this reason it must exist. If a man should try to prove to me by such reasoning that this island truly exists, either I should believe that he was jesting, or I know not which I ought to regard as the greater fool: myself, supposing that I should allow this proof, or him.

Below is an objection from a philosophical exchange, followed by four passages from the same exchange. Which passage is the reply to this objection? Reply with the letter of one option.

Objection: There is a great difference between imagining, that is, having some idea, and conceiving with the mind, that is, inferring as the result of a train of reasoning that something is or exists. But what shall we now say, if reasoning chance to be nothing more than the uniting and stringing together of names or designations by the word 'is'? It will follow that reason gives us no conclusion about the nature of things, but only about the terms that designate them. Thus reasoning will depend on names, names on the imagination, and imagination, perchance, on the motion of the corporeal organs; and so mind will be nothing but the motions in certain parts of an organic body.

A. In reasoning we unite not names but the things signified by the names; and I marvel that the opposite can occur to anyone. For who doubts whether a Frenchman and a German are able to reason in exactly the same way about the same things, though they yet conceive the words in an entirely diverse way? And if my opponent admits that words signify anything, why will he not allow our reasonings to refer to this something that is signified, rather than to the words alone? It will be as correct to infer that earth is heaven as to conclude that mind is motion.
B. Here the meaning assigned to the term idea is merely that of images depicted in the corporeal imagination; and, that being agreed on, it is easy to prove that there is no proper idea of Angel or of God. But I have everywhere shown that I take the term idea to stand for whatever the mind directly perceives. So when I will or when I fear, since at the same time I perceive that I will and fear, that very volition and apprehension are ranked among my ideas. I employed this term because it was the term currently used by philosophers for the forms of perception of the Divine mind, though we can discover no imagery in God.
C. When I say that an idea is innate in us, or imprinted in our souls by nature, I do not mean that it is always present to us. This would make no idea innate. I mean merely that we possess the faculty of summoning up this idea.
D. Although in order to err the faculty of reasoning, or rather of judging, or affirming and denying, is required, because error is a lack of this power, it does not hence follow that this defect is anything real. Just so it does not follow that blindness is anything real, although stones are not said to be blind merely because they are incapable of vision.

Here are two short passages of philosophical argument. In which passage does the conclusion follow from what comes before? Reply with A or B only.

A. The speeds of one and the same body moving in different media are in inverse ratio to the densities of these media. The tenuity of a vacuum differs infinitely from that of any medium filled with matter, however rare. Hence any body which moves through a plenum through a certain space in a certain time ought to move through a vacuum instantaneously. But instantaneous motion is no impossibility. It is therefore impossible that motion should take place through a vacuum.

B. The speeds of one and the same body moving in different media are in inverse ratio to the densities of these media. The tenuity of a vacuum differs infinitely from that of any medium filled with matter, however rare. Hence any body which moves through a plenum through a certain space in a certain time ought to move through a vacuum instantaneously. But instantaneous motion is an impossibility. It is therefore impossible that motion should take place through a vacuum.

Here are two short passages of philosophical argument. In which passage does the conclusion follow from what comes before? Reply with A or B only.

A. The most vehement and intense degree of heat is a very great pain. Some unperceiving things are capable of pain or pleasure. Material substance is a senseless being, not endowed with sense and perception. Therefore material substance cannot be the subject of the greatest heat perceived by sense.

B. Heat at its most violent and intense is a severe pain. Nothing that lacks perception can feel pain or pleasure. Material substance has no senses and no perception. So material substance cannot be what bears the strongest heat that the senses perceive.

Here are two short passages of philosophical argument. In which passage does the conclusion follow from what comes before? Reply with A or B only.

A. Loss of property is a penalty. No penalty is ordained by the divine law for the condition of heresy. It is clear, therefore, that from the standpoint of the divine law property is not forfeited on the ground of heresy.

B. Loss of property is a penalty. No penalty is ordained by the divine law for the condition of heresy. It is clear, therefore, that property is not forfeited on the ground of heresy under any law, divine or human.

Below is an objection from a philosophical exchange, followed by four passages from the same exchange. Which passage is the reply to this objection? Reply with the letter of one option.

Objection: As for my own opinion, I have said more than once that I hold space to be something merely relative, as time is; that I hold it to be an order of coexistences, as time is an order of successions. For space denotes, in terms of possibility, an order of things which exist at the same time, considered as existing together, without enquiring into their manner of existing. And when many things are seen together, one perceives that order of things among themselves.

A. If space was nothing but the order of things coexisting, it would follow that if God should remove in a straight line the whole material world entire, with any swiftness whatsoever, yet it would still always continue in the same place, and that nothing would receive any shock upon the most sudden stopping of that motion. And if time was nothing but the order of succession of created things, it would follow that if God had created the world millions of ages sooner than he did, yet it would not have been created at all the sooner. Further, space and time are quantities, which situation and order are not.
B. The uniformity of space does indeed prove that there could be no external reason why God should create things in one place rather than in another. But does that hinder his own will from being to itself a sufficient reason of acting in any place, when all places are indifferent or alike, and there be good reason to act in some place? In things in their own nature indifferent, mere will, without anything external to influence it, is alone that sufficient reason.
C. It is very true that no two leaves, and perhaps no two drops of water, are exactly alike, because they are bodies very much compounded. But the case is very different in the parts of simple solid matter. And even in compounds, there is no impossibility for God to make two drops of water exactly alike. And if he should make them exactly alike, yet they would never the more become one and the same drop of water because they were alike.
D. Among men, an artificer is justly esteemed the more skilful as his machine will continue longer to move regularly without any farther interposition, because the skill of all human artificers consists only in composing or adjusting certain movements whose principles of motion, such as weights and springs, are altogether independent of the artificer. But with regard to God the case is quite different, because he not only composes or puts things together, but is himself the author and continual preserver of their original forces or moving powers. And consequently it is not a diminution, but the true glory of his workmanship, that nothing is done without his continual government and inspection.

Here are two short passages of philosophical argument. In which passage does the conclusion follow from what comes before? Reply with A or B only.

A. The faculty that produces my ideas of sensible things resides in some substance different from me. This substance is either a body, or God Himself, or some other creature more noble than body. God has given me no faculty to recognise that these ideas come from God or such a creature, but a very great inclination to believe that they are conveyed to me by corporeal objects. Since God is no deceiver, He could not be defended from the accusation of deceit if these ideas were produced by causes other than corporeal objects. Hence we must allow that corporeal things exist.

B. The faculty that produces my ideas of sensible things resides in some substance different from me. This substance is either a body, or God Himself, or some other creature more noble than body. God has given me no faculty to recognise that these ideas come from God or such a creature, but a very great inclination to believe that they are conveyed to me by corporeal objects. Though God is no deceiver, He could be fully defended from the accusation of deceit even if these ideas were produced by causes other than corporeal objects. Hence we must allow that corporeal things exist.

But it now appears that this being than which a greater is inconceivable cannot be conceived not to be, because it exists on so assured a ground of truth. For if it could be conceived not to exist, it could be conceived to have a beginning and an end; but this is impossible.
D. It was more proper to say it cannot be conceived. For although no objects which exist can be understood not to exist, yet all objects, except that which exists in the highest degree, can be conceived not to exist. For all those objects, and those alone, can be conceived not to exist, which have a beginning or end or composition of parts. Be assured, then, that you can conceive of your own non-existence, although you are most certain that you exist.
